note.title: ⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|民主派初選案
note.desc: The largest case ever brought under Hong Kong's National Security Law — 47 pro-democracy figures prosecuted for conspiracy to subvert state power over a 2020 opposition primary election.

pageProps.body:
⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|民主派初選案

Related: ⚖️ Jimmy Lai | Hong Kong Alliance | 🎵 Glory to Hong Kong | 📕 Book Censorship under the NSL

The Hong Kong 47 (民主派初選案) is the largest single prosecution ever brought under the 2020 National Security Law — a case that put nearly the entire front rank of the city's opposition in the dock at once. In the winter of 2021, 47 pro-democracy figures — former lawmakers, district councillors, unionists, a journalist, students and academics — were charged with conspiracy to commit subversion for organising or standing in an unofficial primary election. Their alleged crime was to have tried to win a majority in the Legislative Council through the ballot box. By the time the courts were done, 45 of the 47 had been convicted and jailed for terms of up to 10 years, in a trial held without a jury before judges hand-picked for national-security cases.

The "35+" plan

In July 2020, weeks after the NSL took effect, the pro-democracy camp held a primary election to pick a united slate for that autumn's Legislative Council poll. Despite official warnings that it might breach the new law, more than 600,000 Hong Kong voters turned out over the weekend of 11–12 July 2020 to choose candidates.

The strategy behind it — dubbed "35+" — was authored by legal scholar Benny Tai Yiu-ting (戴耀廷), a co-founder of the 2014 Occupy movement. The opposition had never held a majority in the partly-elected legislature; Tai argued that if democrats could win 35 or more of the 70 seats, they could use the legislature's constitutional powers to veto the government budget. Under the Basic Law, a twice-rejected budget would force the Chief Executive either to dissolve the legislature or to resign — leverage the camp hoped to trade for the 2019 protest movement's "five demands," including universal suffrage.

Prosecutors cast this plan not as ordinary politics but as a plot to paralyse the government and "overthrow" the constitutional order. The trial judges agreed, describing the scheme as a "constitutional mass destruction weapon" aimed at toppling the Hong Kong government.

The trial and verdict

The 47 were charged on 28 February 2021 and most were denied bail, held on remand for years before and during their trial. Of the 47, 31 pleaded guilty and 16 pleaded not guilty, contesting a case heard from early 2023 by three designated national-security judges rather than a jury.

On 30 May 2024, the court convicted 14 of the 16 who had fought the charge and acquitted two — barrister Lawrence Lau Wai-chung (勞偉聰) and district councillor Lee Yue-shun (李予信). Together with the 31 who pleaded guilty, 45 of the 47 stood convicted. The Department of Justice, unhappy with the two acquittals, appealed them.

The sentences (November 2024)

On 19 November 2024 the court handed down sentences ranging from 4 years 2 months to 10 years, sorting the defendants into tiers by their role — "principal organisers," active participants, and others. Those who pleaded guilty received the customary one-third discount; four who testified for the prosecution (Au Nok-hin, Andrew Chiu, Ben Chung and Mike Lam) had their terms cut further.

In September 2026, Joshua Wong — still in prison — pleaded guilty to a separate national-security charge of colluding with foreign forces, exposing him to further years behind bars beyond his primary-case term (CNN).

The appeals

  • 23 February 2026 — The Court of Appeal rejected the appeals of all 12 activists who had challenged their convictions or sentences, endorsing the trial court's "constitutional mass destruction weapon" reasoning. In the same ruling it dismissed the Department of Justice's appeal against Lawrence Lau's acquittal, upholding his not-guilty verdict. Amnesty International called the decision "a missed opportunity to start restoring justice" (HKFP · Al Jazeera · Amnesty).
  • 10 August 2026 — The Court of Appeal granted 11 of the jailed democrats leave to appeal to the Court of Final Appeal, the city's apex court — the first time the case's core national-security questions will be tested at that level. The three appellate judges, led by High Court Chief Judge Jeremy Poon, said the appeals "merit the consideration by the Court of Final Appeal." Among the eleven are Gwyneth Ho and Leung Kwok-hung (HKFP).

By early 2026, some of the shorter-sentenced defendants — credited with years already spent on remand — had begun to be released, even as the longest-serving face years still to run and the final appeal remains pending.

Why it matters

The case criminalised the ordinary machinery of opposition politics — a primary, a manifesto, a plan to win seats and use them. Prosecutors did not allege violence; the "subversion" lay in the intention to win a legislative majority and use its budget veto. That theory, now upheld on appeal, marks how far the NSL has redrawn the limits of dissent: the same years that saw the Hong Kong Alliance convicted for a Tiananmen slogan, ⚖️ Jimmy Lai|黎智英 jailed for his newspaper, and the city's bookshops raided, also saw an entire pro-democracy generation — its scholars, students, unionists and reporters — imprisoned for contesting an election.

noteIndex.title: SHKO(Save Hong Kong Online)
noteIndex.body:
[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law.

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
